abstract.p: Theta oscillations (4-12 Hz) in the hippocampus, driven by synchronous neuronal bursts, are essential for grouping and selecting neuronal ensembles during spatial navigation, memory, and learning (Buzsaki, 2002; Buzsaki et al., 2022). Yet, the specific mechanisms enabling this frequency band to effectively modulate neuronal ensembles remain unclear. Here, we show that burst activity at the CA3-CA1 synapse in the mouse hippocampus initiates rapid activation of astrocytic leaflets. This activation is mediated by retrograde messengers, which in turn activate transient receptor potential channels in astrocytes, potentiating glutamate release from Schaffer collaterals via the activation of presynaptic glutamate receptors. We show that this mechanism is synapse-specific and necessary for the induction of long-term potentiation (LTP). Remarkably, this positive feedback loop peaks 50 to 200 ms after a burst, precisely aligning with the theta frequency range and optimizing reinforcement of neuronal activity. These findings indicate that astrocytes provide critical timing to potentiate synaptic transmission during the initial phases of learning and memory formation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Theta rhythms are electrical oscillations that occur within the brain and play a vital role in a variety of cognitive processes, including memory formation, learning and spatial navigation (Buzsaki, 2002; Buzsaki et al., 2022). Theta oscillations emerge from the synchronous activity of neurons that rhythmically fire in bursts. They are characterized by frequency bands that fall between 4 and 12 Hz and are most prominent in the hippocampus, a region of the brain involved in memory guided behaviors such as spatial navigation or sound manipulation (Vanderwolf, 1969; O’Keefe, 1976; Schiller et al., 2015; Aronov et al., 2017). Several pieces of evidence demonstrate the importance of theta rhythms for memory formation. First, the induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) in the hippocampus is optimal when the time interval between inputs activating neurons is approximately 200 ms (corresponding to ≈ 5Hz, i.e., theta frequency) (Larson et al., 1986; Rose and Dunwiddie, 1986; Buzsaki, 2002; Larson and Munkacsy, 2015). Second, disrupting theta oscillations attenuates associative memory encoding (Winson, 1978; Kota et al., 2020). Third, increasing theta frequency increases performance of animals on a radial maze task, a behavior that relies on the reinforcement of synaptic transmission in the hippocampus (Staubli and Xu, 1995). The reason why theta rhythms are particularly efficient for memory formation remains speculative. Here we propose a potential solution by studying synaptic plasticity in the CA1 region of the hippocampus. We demonstrate that a burst of synaptic inputs produced by Schaffer collateral stimulation, results in a homosynaptic transient potentiation which peaks 50 to 200 ms post burst. This timing, that selectively enhances rhythmic activity occurring at the theta frequencies, is caused by the retrograde activation of neighboring astrocytes that in turn promote the release of neurotransmitter from presynaptic terminals. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the inactivation of this pathway impairs long-term potentiation of the synapse. Overall, our study demonstrates that astrocytes provide the specific timing for the potentiation of synaptic transmission occurring during theta rhythm.

sec.title: Post-burst transient potentiation of Schaffer Collaterals peaks in theta range
sec.p: During learning and spatial navigation, CA3 principal neurons fire action potentials in bursts occurring at particular phases of the theta rhythm (Buzsaki et al., 2022). To determine if and how this activity affects the excitability of CA1 pyramidal neurons, we tested how a single burst of synaptic inputs modulated local synapses by recording the local field potential or membrane current of pyramidal neurons in the CA1 region in response to the stimulation of few Schaffer collaterals (Figure 1a,b). We found that synaptic transmission was transiently enhanced 50 to 300 ms after the burst (Figure 1d). Importantly, three successive bursts occurring at theta frequency produced potentiation with a similar time course (Figure 1c-e), showing that the potentiation can reliably enhance sustained rhythmic activity. The potentiation peaked 50 to 200 ms after the burst (Figure 1d,e), corresponding to frequencies of 4.3-12.5 Hz, i.e., in theta range. The potentiation did not rely on the activation of NMDA receptors as all experiments were done in the presence of the NMDA receptor antagonist AP-5. Additionally, saturating concentrations of the NMDA receptor co-agonist D-serine (100μM) had no impact on the potentiation (Figure S1).

sec.p: To determine if the potentiation was due to a pre- or a postsynaptic mechanism, we compared the responses of pairs of stimuli pre- and post-burst (Figure 1f). We found that the first postburst response was always more potentiated than the second. Consequently, the paired pulse ratio (PPR), calculated as the ratio between the slope of the second and first fEPSP, was decreased (Figure 1fg). This outcome suggests presynaptic potentiation (Zucker and Regehr, 2002). However, as changes in PPR have also been reported to result from postsynaptic-dependent mechanisms (Kirischuk et al., 2002; Heine et al., 2008), we used more robust methods to corroborate our interpretation. We evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in single CA1 pyramidal cells recorded by means of the patch clamp technique (Figure 1h). Here again we found that a burst generated by the stimulation of a few Schaffer collaterals produced a potentiation of synaptic transmission (Figure 1i,j) associated with a decrease in PPR (Figure 1i-k). Because the stimulation intensity was adjusted to be near the threshold for EPSCs, some failures of synaptic transmission occurred (arrow in Figure 1i). However, after the burst, synaptic transmission became more reliable since virtually no failures were present (Figure 1i-l). Moreover, the comparison of the coefficient of variation (CV) of EPSC amplitudes before and after burst stimulation, showed that the average increase in synaptic strength was concomitant with a decrease in relative synaptic noise (Figure 1m), further suggesting presynaptic potentiation (Malinow and Tsien, 1990; Brock et al., 2020). It has been proposed that theta frequencies are optimal for LTP induction due to the disabling of feedforward inhibition that occurs when GABAB receptors inhibit GABA release from interneurons (Larson and Munkacsy, 2015). However, since all patch clamp recordings were performed in the presence of the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (50μM), our results show that the transient potentiation does not involve inhibitory neurons and instead relies on an intrinsic mechanism specific to the CA3-CA1 synapse.

Taken together, these results demonstrate that burst activity of the Schaffer collaterals results in a transient increase in the probability of neurotransmitter release from presynaptic terminals that peaks in a time window corresponding to theta range.

sec.title: Transient potentiation requires astrocytic calcium activity
sec.p: Next, we sought to elucidate the mechanism underlying the transient potentiation of synaptic transmission. We focused on the role of astrocytes for three key reasons: (1) Astrocytes respond to synaptic activity and actively modulate synaptic transmission (Perea and Araque, 2007; Araque et al., 2014; Covelo and Araque, 2018). (2) Astrocytes are important for memory formation (Henneberger et al., 2010; Adamsky et al., 2018; Henneberger et al., 2020; Kol et al., 2020). (3) Although traditionally considered too slow to modulate synaptic activity on a millisecond scale, recent evidence indicates that astrocytes can indeed influence synaptic transmission on time scales comparable to neuronal processes (Lind et al., 2013; Stobart et al., 2018). To test our hypothesis, we first determined if and how fast astrocytes responded to a single burst of stimulation. By monitoring the fluorescent activity of CA1 astrocytes expressing the genetically encoded membrane tethered Ca2+ indicator lck-GcAMP6f (Figure 2a; Figure S2), we found that a single burst of Schaffer collateral stimulation was sufficient to induce Ca2+ responses in astrocyte leaflets (Figure 2bc). Importantly, the earliest Ca2+ responses were detected within 90 ms of the burst (Figure 2c). Given that GcAMP6f has a rise time of 45-80 ms (Chen et al., 2013) and our estimation is based on the time difference between the start of the stimulation and the end of the camera frame exposure, it is likely that astrocytes respond even faster. To determine whether astrocytes played a causal role in the potentiation, we impaired their activation. After positioning a patch pipette containing the Ca2+ chelator BAPTA (40 mM) on the membrane of an astrocyte (Figure 2d), we established that evoked EPSCs in nearby pyramidal neurons were potentiated 100 ms after a single burst of stimulations. Breaking into the astrocyte, thereby loading the local astrocytic network with BAPTA significantly diminished the potentiation (Figure 2ef). After the potentiation was inhibited, the coefficient of variation of EPSC amplitudes increased (Figure 2g), consistent with the removal of a presynaptic potentiation (Malinow and Tsien, 1990; Brock et al., 2020). Collectively, these results demonstrate that astrocytes respond rapidly to a single burst of synaptic activity and that their activation is necessary for the transient potentiation of synaptic transmission.

sec.title: Activation of astrocytic TRP receptors by retrograde signaling causes transient potentiation
sec.p: Because strong dendritic depolarization is the hallmark of burst synaptic activation (Thomas et al., 1998; Remy and Spruston, 2007), we hypothesized that the activation of astrocytes originated from postsynaptic dendrites. We tested this assumption by depolarizing CA1 pyramidal neurons recorded in whole-cell configuration (Figure 2h). Specifically, we found that evoked brief depolarizations mimicking the burst stimulation, induced a transient potentiation of synaptic transmission with a delay corresponding to the theta range (Figure 2ij). This result suggests that the potentiation is activated by retrograde transmission. Here again, we observed failures of synaptic transmission before, but never after the postsynaptic depolarization, although the difference was not statistically significant (Figure 2k). More importantly, the coefficient of variation of EPSP amplitudes increased after postsynaptic depolarization (Figure 2l). These results suggest that postsynaptic depolarization potentiates the release of transmitter from presynaptic terminals and point to a retrograde messenger released from the postsynaptic neuron. The above results imply that the activation of astrocytes in response to Schaffer collateral stimulation would vanish upon the blockade of postsynaptic excitatory synaptic receptors. Consistent with this, we found that the addition of the AMPA-receptor blocker CNQX (10 μM) completely and reversibly eliminated the Ca2+ responses in astrocytes in parallel with postsynaptic responses (Figure 2m,n).

As endocannabinoids (eCBs) released from dendrites are known to activate astrocyte leaflets enwrapping CA3-CA1 synapses (Covelo and Araque, 2018; Robin et al., 2018), we considered them as candidates. We tested this possibility by inhibiting receptors activated by eCBs. We found that blocking cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1) receptors with AM251 did not affect the transient potentiation induced by burst activation of Schaffer collaterals (Fig S1). In addition to CB receptors, eCBs also activate a number of transient receptor potential channels (TRPs)(Muller et al., 2018) expressed by CA1 astrocytes (Butenko et al., 2012; Shigetomi et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2019). TRP channels, which are permeable to cations including Ca2+, may account for the rapid Ca2+ responses observed in astrocytes (Figure 2bc). Since a fraction of TRPs exhibit a strong temperature dependency, with a 10°C temperature coefficient (Q10) of approximately 10–20 (Benham et al., 2003), we tested the sensitivity of the potentiation to temperature changes. We discovered that lowering the bath temperature from near-physiological levels to 25°C eliminated the potentiation while still producing reliable fEPSPs with comparable amplitudes (Figure 3a). The change in temperature notably did not influence paired pulse facilitation (PPF) induced by paired stimulation (Figure 3a). This observation suggests that traditional mechanisms of synaptic facilitation remain unaffected, indicating that burst-mediated potentiation likely relies on a distinct mechanism. We further investigated the role of TRP channels using pharmacological approaches. Given that theta oscillations are diminished in TRPV4-deficient animals (Shibasaki et al., 2015), and that TRPV4 channels are Ca2+-permeable and activated by eCBs (Muller et al., 2018), we identified these channels as promising candidates for further investigation. We found that the TRPV4 antagonist RN-1734 (40 μM) abolished the potentiation (Figure 3bc) concomitant with an increase of synaptic noise compatible with the removal of presynaptic potentiation (Figure 3d). Importantly, the removal of the potentiation produced by RN1734 abolished the temperature sensitivity of the potentiation (Figure 3e). This supports the idea that TRP channels are responsible for the temperature sensitivity of the potentiation and that RN1734 exerts its effects by modulating TRP channel activity. We then tested if it impacted the Ca2+ response of astrocytes. We found that RN1734 strongly reduced the fast Ca2+ responses in astrocytes induced by burst activation of Schaffer collaterals in a reversible manner (Figure 3f). Altogether, these findings suggest that transient potentiation is driven by retrograde activation of astrocytic TRP receptors.

sec.p: We next aimed to identify the gliotransmitter responsible for the observed transient potentiation. Astrocytes are known to release several key gliotransmitters, including D-serine, purines, and glutamate (Araque et al., 2014; de Ceglia et al., 2023). To explore their involvement, we tested the effects of various antagonists and saturating concentrations of these candidates. First, we applied saturating concentrations of D-serine (100 μM). Additionally, we used a cocktail of ATP receptor antagonists, including the non-selective P2 purinergic receptor antagonists suramin (200 μM) and PPADS (100 μM), the P2X4 antagonist BAY-1797 (2 μM), and the P2X7 antagonist KN62 (1 μM). To test for adenosine receptor involvement, we used a combination of the non-selective adenosine receptor antagonist CGS-15943 (1 μM) and the A2A receptor antagonist SCH 58261 (100 nM). None of these treatments reduced the transient potentiation (Figure S1), indicating that neither D-serine nor purines are involved in this process. These negative observations, combined with studies showing that hippocampal astrocytes release glutamate (Covelo and Araque, 2018; de Ceglia et al., 2023), suggest that glutamate is a likely candidate. Addition of the mGluR1 antagonist CPCOEt (60 μM) with the mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (20 μM) and the group II/III mGluR antagonist CPPG (5 μM) did not inhibit the potentiation (Figure S1). Given that AMPA, NMDA, and kainate receptors expressed on presynaptic terminals of Schaffer collaterals modulate neurotransmitter release (Schmitz et al., 2001; McGuinness et al., 2010; Cepeda-Prado et al., 2022), we hypothesized that the transient potentiation is mediated by glutamate acting on presynaptic ionotropic receptors. However, blocking AMPA receptors would not provide conclusive results as it would also inhibit the activation of postsynaptic pyramidal cells (Figure 2m,n). To specifically examine the role of kainate receptors, we applied the antagonist NS-102 (20–40 μM). This treatment partially reduced the transient potentiation without affecting baseline synaptic transmission (Figure 3h-j). Adding a second kainate receptor blocker, ACET (5 μM), alongside NS-102 did not produce any further reduction in potentiation. These results suggest that glutamate acts on presynaptic ionotropic receptors. Considering that NS-102, at the concentration used, has some affinity for AMPA receptors (Verdoorn et al., 1994), and recognizing that all experiments were conducted in the presence of the NMDA receptor antagonist AP-5 (50 μM), it is plausible that astrocyte activation triggers the release of glutamate, which mediates transient potentiation through the activation of all three types of ionotropic glutamate receptors: AMPA, NMDA, and kainate.

sec.title: The transient potentiation is necessary for long-term potentiation
sec.p: Next, we investigated the physiological relevance of the transient potentiation we uncovered. Because it is sustainable across multiple bursts occurring in the theta range (Figure 1ce), because a strong postsynaptic depolarization is necessary for the long-term potentiation (LTP) of synaptic transmission (Nicoll, 2017), because theta is important and optimal for memory formation, and because glutamate released from astrocytes is important for LTP induction (de Ceglia et al., 2023), we hypothesized that the transient potentiation is essential for LTP. A fundamental characteristic of LTP is its input specificity (Gustafsson et al., 1987). We therefore investigated if the potentiation was restricted to active synapses or if it was spreading to their neighbors. For this, we tested if a conditioning burst stimulation applied on a set of Schaffer collaterals affected the response of an adjacent test pathway located less than 50 μm away (Figure 4a). Although the conditioning pathway produced a strong homosynaptic potentiation (Figure 4b), it never promoted the response of neighbor Schaffer collaterals (Figure 4cd). Finally, we tested if the potentiation contributed to the induction of LTP induced by a theta-burst stimulation protocol consisting of 20 bursts applied at 5 Hz (Figure 4e). Because NMDA receptors are necessary for LTP formation at this synapse (Nicoll, 2017), all these experiments were performed in the absence of AP5 in the extracellular medium. We found that synaptic transmission was potentiated during the whole stimulation protocol (Figure 4ef) and remained potentiated for more than one hour (Figure 4gh) in agreement with several previous reports (Hernandez et al., 2005; Larson and Munkacsy, 2015). However, in the presence of RN-1734 the signal exhibited short-term depression during the induction protocol (Figure 4ef) and consequently no LTP was induced (Figure 4gh). Altogether, our results suggest that the transient potentiation provided by the retrograde activation of astrocytes is critical for sustained rhythmic synaptic transmission and the induction of LTP.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In our study, we investigated short-term plasticity at the CA3-CA1 synapse in the hippocampus of adult mice. We observed that burst activation of Schaffer Collaterals resulted in a transient potentiation of excitatory transmission on a time scale corresponding to the theta range. This potentiation was mediated by retrograde messengers, which activated TRP receptors in neighboring astrocytic leaflets, triggering a calcium signal. This process, in turn, enhanced synaptic transmission via glutamate release at the active synapses. Given that this positive feedback loop takes between 50 to 300 ms to complete, it selectively sustains synaptic transmission at theta frequencies, thereby promoting long-term potentiation (LTP).

It is now well established that astrocytes are key contributors to LTP and memory formation as their activation alone can induce LTP and strengthen memory via the sustained release of D-Serine that acts as a NMDA receptor co-agonist (Henneberger et al., 2010; Adamsky et al., 2018).The mechanism we uncovered likely operates at an earlier stage than the sustained released of D-Serine by astrocytes. Specifically, the depolarization of pyramidal dendrites, maintained through retrograde activation of astrocytes, may contribute to the removal of Mg2+ block on postsynaptic NMDA receptors, thus facilitating the induction of LTP. Importantly, we show that the temporal dynamics of astrocyte activation and subsequent gliotransmitter release act as a filter that make hippocampal synapses particularly sensitive to theta rhythm. Theta rhythm in CA1 region is correlated to the reinforcement of specific synapses necessary for the formation of place cells (Buzsaki, 2002; Buzsaki and Moser, 2013; Buzsaki et al., 2022). Our results highlight the crucial role of astrocytes in memory and spatial navigation and suggest that theta frequencies may have been evolutionarily optimized to align with the information processing dynamics of astrocytes.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: All procedures were carried out according to Danish animal welfare legislation. Breeding of mice was approved by the Animal Experiments Inspectorate. Animals were housed under standard conditions in a 12-h day/night cycle (lights on at 7:00). Temperature: 22 °C ± 2 °C. Humidity: 55% ± 10%.

Experiments were performed on 4–8-week-old mice (males and females). Wild type (C57BL/6; Janvier Labs, France) and transgenic mice expressing EGFP under the promoter of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were used. GFAP-EGFP mice (line Tgn(hgFAPEGEP) GFEC 335), were kindly provided by Professor Frank Kirchhoff (University of Saarland, Germany). Data from both strains were similar and pooled for analysis.

sec.title: Slice preparation
sec.p: Mice were decapitated and their brains swiftly dissected submerged in ice-cold carbogen-saturated (95% O2/5% CO2) sucrose-substituted artificial cerebrospinal fluid (sACSF) containing (in mM): 200 Sucrose, 10 D-Glucose. H2O, 26 NaHCO3, 2.5 KCl, 0.5 L-ascorbic acid, 2 Na-pyruvate, 3 myo-inositol, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 0.1 CaCl2, 4 MgCl2. 300 μm thick sagittal slices containing the dorsal hippocampus were made using a Leica vibratome (VT1200, Leica Biosystems; Germany). Brain slices were stored in regular, carbogen-saturated ACSF containing (in mM): 111 NaCl, 11 Glucose, 25 NaHCO3, 3 KCl, 1.1 KH2PO4, 2.5 CaCl2, 1.3 MgCl2 in an interface-style holding chamber at 28 C° for at least 90 min. prior to use. Slices were transferred to a recording chamber for experiments and perfused with 32±1 C° ACSF unless stated otherwise, at a flow rate of ~2.5 mL/min.

sec.title: Local field potentials
sec.p: Brain slices were positioned under the objective of an upright microscope (BX51WI, Olympus; Japan). Local-field potentials (LFP) were recorded by placing an ACSF-filled glass electrode (3-7MΩ) in CA1 Stratum Radiatum (approximately 100 μm from Stratum Pyramidale). Schaffer-collaterals were stimulated by ACSF-filled glass electrodes (~0.5 MΩ) connected to a stimulus isolator (A365; World Precision Instruments; USA) positioned 50-150 μm from the recording electrode. LFP signals were amplified by a MultiClamp700B amplifier (Molecular Devices, USA) and digitized at 20-40 kHz (Digidata 1322a; Molecular Devices, USA). Stimulation intensity was set to 150% of the lowest stimulation intensity that evoked a visible fEPSP. Synaptic responses were quantified by the maximal fEPSP slope across a segment of 0.4 ms (of 0.7 ms for low temperature recordings) along the first half of the fEPSP. Hetero-synaptic potentiation tests were conducted using two stimulation electrodes positioned on either side of the recording electrode. Pathway independence was confirmed by the absence of paired-pulse facilitation between the two pathways (Redondo et al., 2010).

sec.title: Long term potentiation
sec.p: Long term potentiation (LTP) was induced using a bipolar tungsten electrode (TM33CCNON; World Precision Instruments; USA) positioned onto Schaffer collaterals 200-300 μm from a LFP recording electrode. The stimulation was adjusted to the lowest intensity resulting in a population spike. After obtaining a stable baseline fEPSP (1 stimulation / min.), LTP was induced using a theta-burst protocol, which consisted of 20 stimulation bursts delivered at a frequency of 5 Hz, with each burst containing 4 pulses at 100 Hz. Following LTP induction fEPSPs were recorded (1stimulation / min.) for 1 hour.

sec.title: Patch clamp recordings
sec.p: Whole cell patch clamp recordings were conducted on neurons located in CA1 Stratum Pyramidale using glass electrodes (3-7 MΩ) filled with (in mM): 135 K-Gluconate, 10 KCl, 1 MgCl2, 10 HEPES, 2 ATP-N2, 0.014 Alexa 568 (pH adjusted to 7.35 with KOH). The identity of pyramidal cells was confirmed by visually inspecting their somatodendritic arborization with epifluorescent microscopy and by analyzing their electrophysiological profile. Cells with a triangular-shaped soma that exhibited regular firing at frequencies below 30 Hz in response to strong depolarizing current pulses were classified as pyramidal cells. A small number of Schaffer collaterals were stimulated using ACSF-filled glass pipettes (~0.5 MΩ) connected to a stimulus isolator (A365; World Precision Instruments, USA), positioned in the stratum radiatum approximately 50 μm from the apical dendrite. Recordings were conducted using a Multiclamp amplifier (700B; Molecular Devices; USA) and digitized at 20 KHz (Digidata 1440A; Molecular Devices; USA). The stimulation intensity was gradually increased until it evoked EPSCs within the range of 0–40 pA, with a failure rate of less than 50%. For some experiments, whole-cell recordings were performed on EGFP-expressing astrocytes with a BAPTA patch solution containing (in mM): 40 BAPTA-K4, 8 NaCl, 1 MgCl2, 10 HEPES, 2 ATP-N2, 0.014 Alexa 568 (pH adjusted to 7.35).

sec.title: Pharmacology
sec.p: All experiments, unless otherwise specified, were performed in the presence of 50 μM DL-2-Amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (DL-AP-5; HelloBio). The following compounds were bath applied: D-serine (100 μM; HelloBio), Picrotoxin (50 μM; HelloBio), 6-Cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dion (CNQX; 10 μM; HelloBio), 1-(2,4-Dichlorophenyl)-5-(4-iodophenyl)-4-methyl-N-1-piperidinyl-1H-pyrazole-3-carboxamide (AM-251; 100 nM; Tocris), 2,4-Dichloro-N-isopropyl-N-(2-isopropylaminoethyl)benzenesulfonamide (RN-1734; 40 μM; HelloBio), Suramin (200 μM; Sigma-Aldrich), Pyridoxal phosphate-6-azo(benzene-2,4-disulfonic acid) (PPADS; 100 μM; Sigma-Aldrich), N-(4-(3-Chlorophenoxy)-3-sulfamoylphenyl)-2-phenylacetamide, N-[3-(Aminosulfonyl)-4-(3-chlorophenoxy)phenyl]benzeneacetamide (BAY-1797; 2 μM; Sigma-Aldrich), S)-5-Isoquinolinesulfonic acid 4-[2-[(5-isoquinolinylsulfonyl)methylamino]-3-oxo-3-(4-phenyl-1-piperazinyl)propyl]phenyl ester, 1-[N,O-bis(5-Isoquinolinesulfonyl)-N-methyl-L-tyrosyl]-4-phenylpiperazine (KN-62; 1 μM; Sigma-Aldrich), 9-Chloro-2-(2-furanyl)-[1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-c]quinazolin-5-amine (CGS-15943; 1 μM; Sigma-Aldrich), 7-(2-phenylethyl)-5-amino-2-(2-furyl)-pyrazolo-[4,3-e]-1,2,4-triazolo[1,5-c]pyrimidine (SCH 58261; 100 nM; Sigma-Aldrich), 7-Hydroxyiminocyclopropan[b]chromen-1α-carboxylic acid ethyl ester (CPCOEt; 60 μM; Sigma-Aldrich), 6-Methyl-2-(phenylethynyl)pyridine (MPEP; 20 μM; Sigma-Aldrich), (RS)-α-Cyclopropyl-4-phosphonophenyl glycine (CPPG; 5 μM; HelloBio), 5-Nitro-6,7,8,9-tetrahydrobenzo(G)indole-2,3-dione-3-oxime (NS-102; 20-40 μM; MedChemExpress), (S)-1-(2-Amino-2-carboxyethyl)-3-(2-carboxy-5-phenylthiophene-3-yl-methyl)-5-methylpyrimidine-2,4-dione (ACET; 5 μM; HelloBio).

sec.title: Intracranial injection
sec.p: Stereotactic injection of AAV5 pZac2.1 gfaABC1D-lck-GcaMP6f virus (Catalog #52924-AAV5, purchased from Addgene) was carried out in wild-type animals (C57BL6/N, Taconic) at P35-40. Briefly, mice were weighed and subcutaneously injected with 5mg/kg Rimadyl (Carprofen). Mice were anesthetized by placing 1–2 ml of isoflurane (Attane Vet, ScanVet) on a cotton pad inside an isolated chamber. The paw pinch reflex was monitored to confirm the level of anesthesia. Once sufficiently anesthetized, the mouse was transferred to a stereotactic frame, secured on the bite bar, and immobilized with ear bars. Animals were kept anaesthetized under 1L/min O2 and progressively decreasing concentrations of isoflurane for the duration of the experiment (starting from 2%, going down to 0.5%). Eyes were lubricated with a carbomer based lubricant (Vidisic, Bausch & Lomb). The head of the mouse was sterilized by wiping with 70% ethanol and then sprayed 1-2 times with 10mg/spray of lidocaine (Xylocaine®, AstraZeneca) to achieve topical anesthesia. An incision was made at the midline and extended in both anterior and posterior directions to an extent sufficient to view the bregma and lambda positions. The skull was wiped with sterile PBS and then with 50% alcohol using a Q-tip. The stereotactic arm was set to the following coordinates (in relation to Bregma) to target the CA1 area of the dorsal hippocampus: AP: −1.5mm, ML: ± 1mm, DV: −1.55mm. A 1ml syringe attached to a 27G needle was gently rotated at this coordinate to manually drill a hole for the virus injection. A sterile Q-tip dipped in PBS was used to clean the area. The pre-filled microinjection pipette was gently lowered into the brain and 1 μL of 1012 vg/ml virus solution was injected over a period of 5 minutes followed by leaving the micropipette undisturbed for 5 minutes and gently retracting it over a period of 5 minutes. Back-flow of the virus was monitored during this process and adjustments made if necessary. The incision was closed by using veterinary glue (Vetbond, 3M Company) and the mouse was placed on a heating mat until it regained consciousness. The animal was allowed to recover and then gently placed it in its individual cage. Easy access to food and water was provided and the animal was monitored over 3 days.

sec.title: Imaging
sec.p: Calcium imaging was conducted on stratum radiatum astrocytes expressing membrane-targeted lck-GCaMP6s, using an epifluorescence microscope (BX51WI, Olympus, Japan) with LED illumination (X-Cite 120LED, Excelitas; USA). Images were acquired by a sCMOS camera (Zyla 5.5, Andor, UK) at a frame rate of 12.8 fps. Local field potentials were evoked and recorded as previously described.

sec.title: Electrophysiology
sec.p: Electrophysiological data was analyzed using Clampfit 10.7 (Molecular Devices; USA), GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software; USA) and Python3.

sec.title: Image processing
sec.p: Images were extracted as .tif files and analyzed using custom-made python scripts (Python 3.11, perrierlab/Larsen_Hansen_et_al._2024). For bleach correction, the pixels from the calcium time series were split into 100 quantiles based on their average baseline intensity. An exponential decay was fitted to each quantile based only on the baseline before stimulation and the model was subtracted from the relevant pixels for the entire time series. Each quantile was normalized to the average intensity of the first 5 frames of that quantile. The response was quantified as the sum of the maximal and minimal value of the mean response of the entire image after being smoothed by a uniform kernel of length 9 in the first 13 frames (aprox. 1s) following stimulation.

For the images chosen for illustrations, noise was reduced with SUPPORT (statistically unbiased prediction utilizing spatiotemporal information in imaging data) (Eom et al., 2023). The program was trained and applied on the dataset with default parameters except for the temporal window which was reduced to 11. After this, a total variation denoising was applied using the algorithm proposed by (Chambolle, 2004).

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Due to the limited sample sizes of the electrophysiological- and imaging experiments, data was not assumed to be normally distributed. Hence, the non-parametric Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test and Mann-Whitney U rank test were used to assess statistical significance. Significance levels: * = p<0.05, **=p<0.01, *** =p<0.001.

body.p: This important study describes a rapid, short-lived strengthening of communication between hippocampal neurons that appears to depend on signaling through neighboring astrocytes. The electrophysiological evidence for the potentiation itself is solid, but the evidence for the proposed mechanism is incomplete: (1) the timing of the astrocytic Ca2+ signals does not clearly match that of the potentiation, and (2) the conclusion that astrocytes release glutamate onto receptors on the nerve terminal relies on pharmacological experiments that cannot establish where those receptors are located. With additional experimental support, the work would be of interest to neuroscientists studying synaptic plasticity and the interactions between neurons and astrocytes.
Summary:

The manuscript by Larsen et al. aims to show a form of short-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus requiring astrocytic function. They propose a mechanism where postsynaptic AMPA receptor activation induces endocannabinoid signaling onto astrocytes, modulating TRPV4 channels, inducing a rapid Ca2+ signal, which they then propose induces astrocytic glutamate release, targeting presynaptic AMPA/Kainate receptors, thereby enhancing presynaptic release for ~200ms post the induction burst.

The proposed model raises new questions for the field, including the mechanism of astrocytic glutamate release, how astrocyte Ca2+ signaling specifies the output and how it signals release in a synapse-specific manner.
Strengths:

The authors have performed careful electrophysiology to characterize and show the AMPA receptor-dependent presynaptic potentiation using multiple readouts (amplitude, variability, paired pulse). Using pharmacology and changing the recording temperature, the recordings suggest the involvement of astrocytic Ca2+ via TRPV4 receptors. This work builds upon findings in the literature of astrocytic gliotransmitter release (glutamate, D-serine, etc.) and astrocytic modulation of LTP. The novelty of this finding is that it acts with very rapid kinetics, suggesting a highly dynamic interaction between all components of the tripartite synapse.
Weaknesses:

While the authors have done careful electrophysiology and pharmacology to try and establish the mechanism underlying their presynaptic potentiation and the model raises a number of questions that remain unexplored, some of which are beyond the scope of this study. One of the clear open questions in the proposed mechanism is the timing of the astrocytic Ca2+ signaling compared to the neuronal short-term potentiation. The potentiation decays in ~200ms, while the astrocytic Ca2+ signal only reaches its peak ~400ms, taking an extended time to recover. This is potentially due to localized Ca2+ signaling in the leaflet versus more global store-released Ca2+. While localizing the astrocytic Ca2+ imaging is extremely challenging, it also raises questions about how astrocytes can repeatedly respond to multiple neuronal bursts within 200ms of each other, while cytosolic Ca2+ has not recovered.

Secondly, the proposed model has a bit of a leap in attributing the potentiation to presynaptic AMPA receptors. As the authors rightly point out, AMPA receptor activation is required post-syntactically for this potentiation, adding considerable challenge to isolate presynaptic AMPA receptor signaling. The authors show a partial effect by inhibiting kainate receptors, but a lot of the same limitations remain.
Summary:

The authors have discovered that a transient enhancement of synaptic transmission at CA3-CA1 synapses after a short burst of synaptic activity is mediated by astrocytic Ca2+ signalling via a presynaptic mechanism. The authors identify kainate receptors and TRPV4 as part of the signalling cascade controlling the transient potentiation. They also identify that TRPV4 is important for sustained synaptic transmission and its potentiation.
Strengths:
This is a very interesting manuscript. The novelty of the findings and the breadth of potential implications are strengths.
Weaknesses:
A weakness of the present manuscript is the compactness of the presentation and the missing details.

(1) It is a bit unclear how well the time window of potentiation corresponds to the theta range. What were the specific delays in the experiments (e.g. in Figure 1a-e)? The potentiation appears to be very prominent/strongest at 40 ms (?), which corresponds to ~ 25 Hz (well above the theta range). The time course of the Ca2+ response in Figure 2a-c is, on its own, as the authors point out, not suitable for gauging the Ca2+ signal shape in the absence of the indicator. Was this a single imaging experiment (n = 1)?

(2) The experiments presented in Figure S1 seem underpowered given the large variability in experimental outcomes (e.g. ATP cocktail, mGluR cocktail, D-serine) and their importance for the authors' conclusions. Have the authors tested the effects for statistical significance and, if so, how? Presumably the experiments with D-serine were not performed in the presence of APV, as mentioned in the main text?

(3) The statements about GABAergic inhibition are a bit unclear (lines 90 - 95). Inhibition of GABA-A receptors does not suppress GABA release from interneurons after activation of excitatory axons. The direct experiment would be to inhibit GABA-B receptors (located, for instance, on presynaptic terminals, astrocytes, etc.) to test that these do not play a role.

(4) It is difficult to follow the line of argument about glutamate release (lines 259-268). In the experiments with NS-102, the kainate receptors mediating part of the potentiation could also be on interneurons (or elsewhere). I could not find the data corresponding to the stated lack of an effect of NS-102 on baseline transmission, and the absence of an effect of ACET on top of that of NS-102 also does not seem to be illustrated/documented.

(5) The discussion feels very focused and compact. For example, the present study is mostly based on pharmacology and many of the involved signalling components (e.g. TRPV4, kainate receptors) can be located in various cellular compartments (e.g. excitatory neurons, interneurons, pre- and postsynaptic sites, astrocytes). The manuscript could benefit from a more in-depth discussion in that direction. The question of whether astrocytes release glutamate has also received a lot of attention, which could be brought to the attention of the reader. More importantly, there is already literature on how astrocytes are engaged and contribute to theta-range activity and how that is relevant to learning: (Wang et al., 2009) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638986/, Fig. 5.3) and (Sardinha et al., 2017; Bohmbach et al., 2022). These studies seem to be relevant to both the Introduction and Discussion.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

The manuscript by Larsen et al. aims to show a form of short-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus requiring astrocytic function. They propose a mechanism where postsynaptic AMPA receptor activation induces endocannabinoid signaling onto astrocytes, modulating TRPV4 channels, inducing a rapid Ca2+ signal, which they then propose induces astrocytic glutamate release, targeting presynaptic AMPA/Kainate receptors, thereby enhancing presynaptic release for ~200ms post the induction burst.

The proposed model raises new questions for the field, including the mechanism of astrocytic glutamate release, how astrocyte Ca2+ signaling specifies the output and how it signals release in a synapse-specific manner.
Strengths:

The authors have performed careful electrophysiology to characterize and show the AMPA receptor-dependent presynaptic potentiation using multiple readouts (amplitude, variability, paired pulse). Using pharmacology and changing the recording temperature, the recordings suggest the involvement of astrocytic Ca2+ via TRPV4 receptors. This work builds upon findings in the literature of astrocytic gliotransmitter release (glutamate, D-serine, etc.) and astrocytic modulation of LTP. The novelty of this finding is that it acts with very rapid kinetics, suggesting a highly dynamic interaction between all components of the tripartite synapse.
Weaknesses:

While the authors have done careful electrophysiology and pharmacology to try and establish the mechanism underlying their presynaptic potentiation and the model raises a number of questions that remain unexplored, some of which are beyond the scope of this study. One of the clear open questions in the proposed mechanism is the timing of the astrocytic Ca2+ signaling compared to the neuronal short-term potentiation. The potentiation decays in ~200ms, while the astrocytic Ca2+ signal only reaches its peak ~400ms, taking an extended time to recover. This is potentially due to localized Ca2+ signaling in the leaflet versus more global store-released Ca2+. While localizing the astrocytic Ca2+ imaging is extremely challenging, it also raises questions about how astrocytes can repeatedly respond to multiple neuronal bursts within 200ms of each other, while cytosolic Ca2+ has not recovered.

body.p: We plan to collect additional two-photon imaging data to characterize the time course of calcium signals in individual astrocytic leaflets with higher spatial and temporal resolution.

disp-quote.p: Secondly, the proposed model has a bit of a leap in attributing the potentiation to presynaptic AMPA receptors. As the authors rightly point out, AMPA receptor activation is required post-syntactically for this potentiation, adding considerable challenge to isolate presynaptic AMPA receptor signaling. The authors show a partial effect by inhibiting kainate receptors, but a lot of the same limitations remain.

body.p: We will perform additional experiments to determine whether presynaptic AMPA receptors enhance glutamate release from Schaffer collateral terminals.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

The authors have discovered that a transient enhancement of synaptic transmission at CA3-CA1 synapses after a short burst of synaptic activity is mediated by astrocytic Ca2+ signalling via a presynaptic mechanism. The authors identify kainate receptors and TRPV4 as part of the signalling cascade controlling the transient potentiation. They also identify that TRPV4 is important for sustained synaptic transmission and its potentiation.
Strengths:
This is a very interesting manuscript. The novelty of the findings and the breadth of potential implications are strengths.
Weaknesses:
A weakness of the present manuscript is the compactness of the presentation and the missing details.

(1) It is a bit unclear how well the time window of potentiation corresponds to the theta range. What were the specific delays in the experiments (e.g. in Figure 1a-e)? The potentiation appears to be very prominent/strongest at 40 ms (?), which corresponds to ~ 25 Hz (well above the theta range). The time course of the Ca2+ response in Figure 2a-c is, on its own, as the authors point out, not suitable for gauging the Ca2+ signal shape in the absence of the indicator. Was this a single imaging experiment (n = 1)?

body.p: The timing of the test stimulations in Figure 1 is expressed as the delay following the burst. Each burst consisted of four stimuli delivered at 100 Hz and therefore lasted 30 ms. We systematically tested post-burst delays of 20, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 500, and 1000 ms. When expressed as the interval from the onset of the burst to the test stimulus, these delays correspond to frequencies of 20.0, 12.5, 7.7, 5.6, 4.3, 3.6, 3.0, 1.9, and 1.0 Hz, respectively. Accordingly, post-burst delays of 50–200 ms correspond to stimulation frequencies of 12.5–4.3 Hz, which fall within the theta-frequency range (green shaded area in fig. 1b and 1f). We have clarified this point in the legend to Figure 1 and in the method section.

Following three bursts, no potentiation was observed at a post-burst delay of 20 ms (corresponding to 20 Hz). In contrast, clear potentiation emerged at 50 ms (12.5 Hz) and reached its maximum at 150 ms (5.6 Hz), placing both the onset and peak of the potentiation well within the theta-frequency range.
Calcium imaging data illustrated in Figure 2a-c were obtained in 6 slices. This point in now clarified in the figure legend.
We plan to collect additional two-photon imaging data to characterize the time course of calcium signals in individual astrocytic leaflets with higher spatial and temporal resolution.

disp-quote.p: (2) The experiments presented in Figure S1 seem underpowered given the large variability in experimental outcomes (e.g. ATP cocktail, mGluR cocktail, D-serine) and their importance for the authors' conclusions. Have the authors tested the effects for statistical significance and, if so, how? Presumably the experiments with D-serine were not performed in the presence of APV, as mentioned in the main text?

body.p: The experiments with D-Serine were done in the absence of APV. This point was added to the figure legend.

disp-quote.p: (3) The statements about GABAergic inhibition are a bit unclear (lines 90 - 95). Inhibition of GABA-A receptors does not suppress GABA release from interneurons after activation of excitatory axons. The direct experiment would be to inhibit GABA-B receptors (located, for instance, on presynaptic terminals, astrocytes, etc.) to test that these do not play a role.

body.p: We will revise and clarify our statement about the lack of effect of GABAA receptor blockade:

“It has been proposed that theta frequency is optimal for LTP induction because an initial burst transiently suppresses feedforward inhibition through activation of presynaptic GABAB receptors on inhibitory terminals, thereby reducing GABA release onto pyramidal-cell GABAA receptors and maximizing postsynaptic depolarization during a subsequent burst delivered ~200 ms later (Larson and Munkacsy, 2015). This mechanism predicts that blocking GABAA receptors should occlude the contribution of feedforward disinhibition to theta-frequency-dependent potentiation. However, since all patch clamp recordings in our study were performed in the presence of the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (50µM). The persistence of transient potentiation under these conditions therefore indicates that it does not require GABAA receptor-mediated inhibition and instead reflect a mechanism intrinsic to the CA3-CA1 synapse.”

disp-quote.p: (4) It is difficult to follow the line of argument about glutamate release (lines 259-268). In the experiments with NS-102, the kainate receptors mediating part of the potentiation could also be on interneurons (or elsewhere). I could not find the data corresponding to the stated lack of an effect of NS-102 on baseline transmission, and the absence of an effect of ACET on top of that of NS-102 also does not seem to be illustrated/documented.

body.p: All patch clamp recordings in our study were performed in the presence of the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (50µM) discarding the involvement of interneurons in the potentiation.
We will add data to the legend of Figure 3H indicating that NS-102 had no effect on baseline synaptic transmission.

disp-quote.p: (5) The discussion feels very focused and compact. For example, the present study is mostly based on pharmacology and many of the involved signalling components (e.g. TRPV4, kainate receptors) can be located in various cellular compartments (e.g. excitatory neurons, interneurons, pre- and postsynaptic sites, astrocytes). The manuscript could benefit from a more in-depth discussion in that direction. The question of whether astrocytes release glutamate has also received a lot of attention, which could be brought to the attention of the reader. More importantly, there is already literature on how astrocytes are engaged and contribute to theta-range activity and how that is relevant to learning: (Wang et al., 2009) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638986/, Fig. 5.3) and (Sardinha et al., 2017; Bohmbach et al., 2022). These studies seem to be relevant to both the Introduction and Discussion.
